THOUGHT: This 8-year-old girl developed a low-grade fever, pruritic rash, and generalized joint pain one week after starting amoxicillin for acute sinusitis. The rash began in flexural areas (antecubital and popliteal fossae) — a classic distribution for serum sickness–like reaction (SSLR) — and then spread to the trunk and distal extremities. Physical exam reveals erythematous annular plaques with central clearing (targetoid or “iris” lesions), which can be seen in SSLR (though more classically associated with erythema multiforme, the timing and drug exposure make SSLR more likely here). Periorbital edema is a hallmark feature of SSLR, reflecting systemic immune complex–mediated vasculitis. Joint pain (arthralgias) without frank arthritis (no swelling or warmth) is also characteristic of SSLR. The absence of mucosal involvement, normal urinalysis (no proteinuria or hematuria to suggest renal involvement), and lack of severe systemic toxicity argue against more serious conditions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome, vasculitis (e.g., IgA vasculitis/HSP), or systemic lupus erythematosus. While HSP (IgA vasculitis) is common in this age group and can present with rash, arthralgias, and low-grade fever, it typically features palpable purpura (not annular plaques), lower-extremity predominance, and often gastrointestinal or renal involvement — none of which are present here. The temporal relationship to amoxicillin (a known trigger of SSLR), the triad of fever, rash, and arthralgias, and the presence of periorbital edema strongly support serum sickness–like reaction over other differential diagnoses.

DIAGNOSIS: Serum sickness–like reaction
